title: JSON
summary: JSON is a text format that lets programs exchange simple data.

subtopics.title: Data shape
subtopics.explanation: JSON supports strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays, and objects. It does not support functions or `undefined`. It is like a small set of building blocks for describing data. Knowing the supported types helps you avoid trying to send JavaScript behavior through a data format. For example, a server response may be valid JSON but contain a string where the app expects a number. In practice, parse a response body only after checking whether the request succeeded.

subtopics.title: Read text
subtopics.explanation: `JSON.parse()` turns valid JSON text into a JavaScript value. The text must follow JSON syntax exactly. It is like reading a form written in an agreed format. Parsing can throw an error when text is broken, so handle that failure when reading user input or network responses. For example, wrap parsing of editable local text in error handling. In practice, catch a syntax error when a user imports malformed JSON text.

subtopics.title: Write text
subtopics.explanation: `JSON.stringify()` turns supported JavaScript data into JSON text. It is useful when saving data or sending it over a network. It is like packing a structured form into a message. Some JavaScript values are omitted or transformed, so do not assume every object survives a round trip unchanged. For example, stringify a small preference object before storing it in localStorage. In practice, stringify a small preferences object before storing it locally.

subtopics.title: JSON rules
subtopics.explanation: JSON strings and property names use double quotes. Values cannot contain comments, trailing commas, or unquoted property names. It is like following a strict form template. A JSON file may be rejected even when it looks close to JavaScript object syntax. For example, undefined object properties may be omitted when text is generated. In practice, check parsed fields because valid syntax can still contain the wrong data.

subtopics.title: Handle invalid input
subtopics.explanation: Parsing only proves the text follows JSON grammar; it does not prove the data has the fields your app needs. Check the shape and values before relying on them. It is like opening a correctly addressed package that may still contain the wrong item. Use runtime validation for important external data. For example, validate required fields after parsing instead of trusting the parse result. In practice, a function property does not become transferable JSON data.

foundations.overview: JSON is a text format for exchanging structured data between programs. It represents values such as strings, numbers, arrays, and objects using strict punctuation rules. Think of it like a form both sides agree how to read. JavaScript can parse JSON text into values and turn supported values back into text. Validate data from outside your app because valid JSON can still contain unexpected information.
foundations.whyItMatters: JSON is a common data boundary. Parsing checks syntax; validation checks whether the resulting values meet the application’s requirements.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser exposes a global JSON object with parse and stringify implemented in native code for speed. fetch responses provide a .json() helper that reads the body text and parses it for you.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Reading API responses (await res.json()), sending request bodies (body: JSON.stringify(payload)), persisting state to localStorage, and loading configuration files.
foundations.businessImpact: Reliable serialization keeps client and server in sync; silent data loss from JSON deep-copy or invalid payloads causes user-facing bugs and failed transactions.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding valid JSON and stringify's quirks prevents corrupted payloads, broken localStorage state, and crashes from unhandled parse errors.
foundations.performanceImpact: stringify/parse are fast but synchronous; serializing very large objects can block the main thread. Cache parsed results and avoid re-serializing unchanged data in hot paths.
commonUseCases: Parsing API responses with JSON.parse or response.json()
Persisting and reading app state in localStorage
Quick (lossy) deep copies — prefer structuredClone for safety
Read a JSON response from an API.
Save a simple preference object in browser storage.
Display a helpful error when imported text is malformed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: JSON and a JavaScript object are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: JSON is a text string with restricted types; a JS object is a live in-memory value. You convert between them with stringify and parse.

commonMisconceptions.myth: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) is a safe deep copy.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It drops functions, undefined, and symbols, turns Dates into strings, and breaks Map/Set — use structuredClone() for a faithful copy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: JSON.parse checks that the object matches your interface.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It checks syntax only; validate the resulting value’s shape and constraints.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every JavaScript value survives stringify and parse unchanged.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Functions, undefined, special numbers, and object identity do not round-trip as ordinary JSON data.

visualExplorer.title: Round-tripping data through JSON
visualExplorer.caption: Step through turning a JavaScript object into a JSON string and back, seeing what changes along the way.

config.intro: Follow a user object through JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.

steps.name: Start with an object
steps.detail: A live JS object: { name: 'Ada', joined: new Date(), greet: () => 'hi' }.

steps.name: Call JSON.stringify
steps.detail: The object is serialized to a text string; the Date becomes an ISO string and the greet function is dropped.

steps.name: Send or store the string
steps.detail: The JSON string can travel over the network or sit in localStorage — it's just text now.

steps.name: Call JSON.parse
steps.detail: The string is read back into a new JS object with name and joined (as a string), but no greet function.

steps.name: Use the result
steps.detail: You now have a fresh object — a deep copy of the JSON-representable parts, missing anything JSON can't encode.

interactiveExamples.title: stringify and parse round-trip
interactiveExamples.explanation: Convert an object to a JSON string and back. Notice the string is text, and parsing gives a brand-new object.

interactiveExamples.title: What stringify drops, and a reviver
interactiveExamples.explanation: Functions and undefined are dropped; a reviver can transform values (here, turning an ISO string back into a Date).

codeLab.title: Safe parse helper
codeLab.instructions: Write safeParse(text) that returns the parsed value if `text` is valid JSON, or null if parsing fails (instead of throwing). Use a try/catch so callers never crash on bad input.
hints: Return null from the catch block so invalid input doesn't throw.

keyTakeaways: JSON supports strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays, and objects.
JSON strings and property names use double quotes.
Parsing only proves the text follows JSON grammar; it does not prove the data has the fields your app needs.
